Agent share

Per-agent prevalence under both valid denominators. Repositories can carry more than one agent.

Paired prevalence plot · point estimate with 95% Wilson interval

Preparing visual…

How to read “Agent share”

Headline measure

How widely is each coding agent observed across the repositories in this corpus?

What you are looking at

This compares two prevalence estimates for the same agents. The scanned denominator includes every repository in the frozen detection run; the readable denominator keeps only repositories with a usable detection document. The distance between the two dots shows how much non-analysable repositories affect the headline. Prevalence here means “evidence was observed”, not “the developer says they use it”.

How to read it

  1. Each row is one agent; the two dots are the scanned and readable estimates.
  2. Horizontal position is a percentage. A dot further right means more repositories with observed evidence.
  3. Whiskers are 95% intervals. Overlapping intervals mean the ordering of close agents is not reliable.
  4. Rows are sorted for readability, so compare values rather than rank alone.
  5. A repository can count toward several agents, so shares may sum past 100%.

For example. An agent at 12% on both dots has evidence in roughly 12 of every 100 repositories under each denominator. A much lower readable estimate would mean unreadable repositories were disproportionately important to the scanned number.

Key terms in this figure

Coding agent
A named AI coding tool or assistant tracked by the corpus. One repository can show evidence for several agents.
Eligible frame
The repositories this run can legitimately analyse: a usable detection document exists and every selected detection channel succeeded. Repositories outside the frame stay visible in coverage tables but do not enter adoption denominators.
95% Wilson interval
A range around an observed share that accounts for sample size. Small denominators produce wide intervals; a wide interval means the exact value is uncertain.
Detection channel
One way the scanner looks for agent evidence, such as a committed config file, an author or commit trailer, or pull-request metadata. Different channels see different parts of the same usage.

Keep in mind. These are observed traces, not a survey of developer intent. An agent used without leaving a detectable trace is invisible here.

Shared markers and content fallbacks

AGENTS.md and similar shared conventions stay visible but are excluded from every agent count.

Lollipop frequency plot · shared markers are not products; content fallbacks are used only when no named agent exists

Repositories with shared markers 0
Content-only attributions 0

Preparing visual…

How to read “Shared markers and content fallbacks”

Validity diagnostic

How much shared, vendor-neutral evidence exists, and how is it kept out of the agent counts?

What you are looking at

Some evidence does not identify a product. An AGENTS.md file, an “AI Assistant” author identity, or an “ai-generated” pull-request label shows that a repository participates in an AI convention without saying which agent is used. Treating that evidence as an agent would create a phantom product and inflate every adoption share. The top dataset lists these shared markers; the second dataset, when present, lists agents inferred from a single explicit addressee inside a shared file.

How to read it

  1. Each lollipop is one marker and the number of repositories that show it.
  2. Colour groups the marker by source: file, author identity, or label.
  3. Switch datasets with the selector: shared markers are the common case; content fallbacks are rare and always marked as such.
  4. Shared markers never appear in agent prevalence, agent counts, or adoption denominators.
  5. A repository can carry several markers, so marker counts are not mutually exclusive.

For example. If AGENTS.md appears in 1,200 repositories but no product is named, those repositories show a shared marker and zero agents. The lollipop records the practice without adding 1,200 phantom adopters.

Key terms in this figure

Shared marker
Evidence of a convention rather than a product: AGENTS.md, an “AI Assistant” identity, or an “ai-generated” label. Shared markers are shown for completeness but never counted as agent adoption.
Coding agent
A named AI coding tool or assistant tracked by the corpus. One repository can show evidence for several agents.
Detection channel
One way the scanner looks for agent evidence, such as a committed config file, an author or commit trailer, or pull-request metadata. Different channels see different parts of the same usage.

Keep in mind. A missing marker is not evidence of absence: a repository may use an agent without committing an AGENTS.md file or using a labelled identity. Content fallbacks are conservative and deliberately cover only files that address exactly one named agent.

Agents by country

Country–agent structure, normalized by readable repositories within each country.

Prevalence matrix · cell color encodes share; text gives exact percent and count

Preparing visual…

How to read “Agents by country”

Headline measure

Which agents appear in which countries, and where are they concentrated?

What you are looking at

Rows are countries and columns are agents. Each cell divides repositories with evidence for that agent by all readable repositories from that country, so large and small countries can be compared on the same scale. The matrix maps this corpus; it is not a representative sample of the world's developers.

How to read it

  1. Read across a row to compare agents within one country.
  2. Read down a column to compare one agent across countries.
  3. Darker cells and larger numbers mean a larger share; the n column is the row denominator.
  4. Hover a cell for the exact percentage and repository count.
  5. Treat strong colours in rows with small n as noisy evidence.

For example. A cell showing 18% with n=250 means 45 of that country's 250 readable repositories carried evidence for that agent.

Key terms in this figure

Coding agent
A named AI coding tool or assistant tracked by the corpus. One repository can show evidence for several agents.
Eligible frame
The repositories this run can legitimately analyse: a usable detection document exists and every selected detection channel succeeded. Repositories outside the frame stay visible in coverage tables but do not enter adoption denominators.
Unknown stratum
Missing or unresolved metadata is kept as its own group, usually labelled “Unknown”, instead of being dropped or silently treated as zero.

Keep in mind. Country is the owner's public location, not where the code is written. Organization-owned repositories are attributed to the organization's registered country.

Agent use

Observed repositories partitioned by ordered commit-intensity tier.

Normalized composition strip · mutually exclusive tiers sum to 100%

Eligible prevalence 100.0%
Scanned prevalence 100.0%
Unavailable 0

Preparing visual…

How to read “Agent use”

Headline measure

What mix of commit-intensity tiers does the observed corpus show?

What you are looking at

The bar divides observed repositories into ordered tiers based on the share of eligible commits attributed to an agent: none, limited, moderate, or pervasive. It is a composition chart, so the whole bar is one denominator and the segments are mutually exclusive. The statistic strip repeats the same picture for the eligible and scanned frames.

How to read it

  1. The leftmost segment is the lowest intensity, usually no observed agent use; the rightmost is pervasive use.
  2. Segment width is that tier's share of repositories, so the widths add to 100%.
  3. Hover a segment for its exact share and count.
  4. Use “Unavailable” in the stat strip to see how much of the frame could not be classified.
  5. Open the adoption-intensity panel for the full distribution among adopters.

For example. If “No agent” fills 55% of the bar, just under half of the observed frame shows at least some agent evidence; the remaining segments show how heavy that use is.

Key terms in this figure

Commit ratio
The share of eligible inspected commits attributed to an agent. Commits that cannot be attributed, and merge commits where the scanner excludes them, stay outside the denominator.
Pervasive use
At least 20% of eligible inspected commits were attributed to an agent. The threshold is a reporting convention, not a natural boundary.
Eligible frame
The repositories this run can legitimately analyse: a usable detection document exists and every selected detection channel succeeded. Repositories outside the frame stay visible in coverage tables but do not enter adoption denominators.
Coding agent
A named AI coding tool or assistant tracked by the corpus. One repository can show evidence for several agents.

Keep in mind. The tiers describe attributed commits inside the inspected window. They do not measure the share of code written by AI or the importance of the agent to the project.

Agent use by country

Repo-weighted prevalence; unresolved owners remain visible as Unknown.

Caterpillar forest plot · point estimate with 95% Wilson interval

Preparing visual…

How to read “Agent use by country”

Headline measure

How does agent-use prevalence differ across countries?

What you are looking at

Each row is a country with at least one eligible repository. The estimate is repo-weighted, so every eligible repository counts once regardless of owner. Countries with few repositories get wide intervals, which is the main reason two similar point estimates may not be meaningfully different.

How to read it

  1. Move down the rows to compare countries; the dot is the point estimate.
  2. The horizontal line is a 95% interval, and a triangle marks fewer than 10 eligible repositories.
  3. Look at interval width before comparing small differences between dots.
  4. Treat overlapping intervals as compatible with the same underlying rate.
  5. Use the data tables for exact counts and the unsorted country list.

For example. Two countries at 20% and 24% with overlapping intervals should be read as similar. A four-point gap with narrow, non-overlapping intervals is stronger evidence of a difference in this corpus.

Key terms in this figure

95% Wilson interval
A range around an observed share that accounts for sample size. Small denominators produce wide intervals; a wide interval means the exact value is uncertain.
Repo-weighted
Every eligible repository counts equally. An owner with 500 repositories contributes 500 times as much as a single-repository owner.
Eligible frame
The repositories this run can legitimately analyse: a usable detection document exists and every selected detection channel succeeded. Repositories outside the frame stay visible in coverage tables but do not enter adoption denominators.
Unknown stratum
Missing or unresolved metadata is kept as its own group, usually labelled “Unknown”, instead of being dropped or silently treated as zero.

Keep in mind. These are repo-weighted country associations, not representative national estimates. Repositories cluster within owners, so the intervals understate real-world dependence.

Repository size

Prevalence across frozen disk-size bands; choose an agent to inspect its profile.

Ordered stratum profile · point estimate with 95% Wilson interval

Preparing visual…

How to read “Repository size”

Headline measure

Does agent use change with repository size?

What you are looking at

Repositories are grouped into frozen disk-size bands. The chart shows whether larger codebases are more or less likely to carry agent evidence. Size is measured once from the source snapshot, so later edits do not change a repository's band.

How to read it

  1. The horizontal axis runs from smaller to larger size bands.
  2. Choose “Any signal” or a specific agent from the selector.
  3. The dot is prevalence and the whisker is its 95% interval.
  4. A flat profile means size is a weak differentiator; a steady slope means use rises or falls with size.
  5. A gap in the line means the band had no eligible repositories.

For example. If prevalence climbs steadily from the smallest to the largest band while the intervals stay narrow, large repositories are more likely to show agent evidence. If the intervals overlap heavily, the pattern is weak.

Key terms in this figure

Eligible frame
The repositories this run can legitimately analyse: a usable detection document exists and every selected detection channel succeeded. Repositories outside the frame stay visible in coverage tables but do not enter adoption denominators.
95% Wilson interval
A range around an observed share that accounts for sample size. Small denominators produce wide intervals; a wide interval means the exact value is uncertain.
Coding agent
A named AI coding tool or assistant tracked by the corpus. One repository can show evidence for several agents.

Keep in mind. Disk size is a rough proxy for project scale. It includes vendored code, generated files, and assets, so it is not a measure of team size or code complexity.

Agent debuts

Earliest repository creation and earliest observed signal inside this run's bounded window.

Paired event timeline · endpoints are bounded earliest observations, not true debuts

Preparing visual…

How to read “Agent debuts”

Headline measure

When do agents first become visible in this corpus?

What you are looking at

For each agent, the line runs from the earliest creation date among repositories carrying it to the earliest observed signal in this run. Both endpoints are bounded by what the run could see. The left endpoint describes the repositories; the right endpoint describes the first observed trace.

How to read it

  1. Each row is one agent; the left endpoint is earliest repository creation.
  2. The right endpoint is the earliest observed signal date for that agent.
  3. A long line means the agent appeared on repositories that had already existed for a while.
  4. The repos and dated columns show how many repositories support the row.
  5. Rows are chronological, so rows near the top are the earliest observations.

For example. A line that starts in 2019 and ends in 2024 does not mean the agent existed in 2019. It means the agent was first observed in this run on repositories created as early as 2019.

Key terms in this figure

Bounded date
The earliest date observable inside this run's window. It is not an agent's true first use.
Coding agent
A named AI coding tool or assistant tracked by the corpus. One repository can show evidence for several agents.
Coverage
The share of repositories for which a measure could actually be computed. It tells you whether a denominator is trustworthy, not whether adoption is high.

Keep in mind. Earliest observed signal is not true first use. Public visibility, repository sampling, and channel coverage can all hide earlier adoption.

Fingerprint prevalence

Choose an agent to compare its strongest repository-visible fingerprints.

Lollipop frequency plot · top five fingerprints per agent by repository count

Preparing visual…

How to read “Fingerprint prevalence”

Headline measure

Which concrete repository traces identify an agent?

What you are looking at

A fingerprint is a repository-visible marker linked to one detection channel, such as a config filename, dependency, or commit pattern. The chart ranks the five fingerprints found in the most repositories for the selected agent. It describes the detection surface, not the agent's capabilities or the quality of its use.

How to read it

  1. Select an agent from the selector.
  2. Each bar counts repositories where that fingerprint appeared; a longer bar means a more widespread trace.
  3. The tooltip names the channel and the earliest observed date for that fingerprint.
  4. Fingerprints overlap, so one repository can contribute to several bars.
  5. Compare mixes across agents to see which traces dominate each agent's evidence.

For example. If a config-file fingerprint leads with 800 repositories and a commit-trailer fingerprint follows with 120, the agent is mostly detected through committed configuration in this corpus.

Key terms in this figure

Fingerprint
A concrete repository-visible trace, such as a specific config filename, dependency marker, or commit pattern, linked to one detection channel.
Detection channel
One way the scanner looks for agent evidence, such as a committed config file, an author or commit trailer, or pull-request metadata. Different channels see different parts of the same usage.
Coding agent
A named AI coding tool or assistant tracked by the corpus. One repository can show evidence for several agents.

Keep in mind. Fingerprints reveal detectable traces, not depth of use. A widely copied config can outrank meaningful but sparsely documented adoption.

Country wealth vs agent use

Log GDP per capita against repo-weighted adoption. Descriptive, never causal.

Bubble scatterplot · unweighted OLS fit on eligible countries; area encodes readable n

Pearson r —
Spearman ρ —
pp per GDP doubling —
Pearson bootstrap 95% —
Pearson leave-one-out —
Countries in fit 0
Minimum n 10

Preparing visual…

How to read “Country wealth vs agent use”

Headline measure

Do countries with higher GDP per capita also show higher agent adoption?

What you are looking at

Each bubble is a country. GDP per capita comes from a country-level economic series matched to the owner's country, and adoption is repo-weighted within that country. The fitted line is unweighted, so each qualifying country contributes one point regardless of how many repositories it has.

How to read it

  1. Horizontal position is GDP per capita on a log scale; vertical position is observed adoption.
  2. Bubble area reflects readable repository count, and the whisker is the country's 95% interval.
  3. The straight line is a least-squares fit across countries above the minimum-size threshold.
  4. A positive slope means richer countries show higher adoption in this corpus.
  5. Tooltips flag influential countries by Cook's distance; check whether removing one country changes the story.

For example. A fit rising from about 8% at $10k GDP per capita to 25% at $50k is a positive ecological association. It is not evidence that raising income raises adoption.

Key terms in this figure

GDP per capita
A country-level economic measure matched to the repository owner's country. It describes the country, not the individual developer.
Repo-weighted
Every eligible repository counts equally. An owner with 500 repositories contributes 500 times as much as a single-repository owner.
95% Wilson interval
A range around an observed share that accounts for sample size. Small denominators produce wide intervals; a wide interval means the exact value is uncertain.

Keep in mind. Country-level association cannot establish causation and can be driven by a handful of countries. The bootstrap and leave-one-out ranges show how fragile the fit is.

Creation cohorts

Cross-sectional prevalence by repository creation cohort; cutoff 2025-01-01.

Ordered cohort profile · 95% Wilson intervals for binomial outcomes

Preparing visual…

How to read “Creation cohorts”

Headline measure

Is agent use different in older versus newer repositories?

What you are looking at

Repositories are grouped by creation date: the installed base before the study cutoff and quarterly cohorts after it. This is a cross-sectional snapshot, not a longitudinal study that follows the same repositories over time. Cohort differences mix age with selection into the corpus.

How to read it

  1. Cohorts run from oldest to newest along the horizontal axis.
  2. Each line is an evidence definition: any signal, committed configuration, or recent commit use.
  3. Dots are prevalence and whiskers are 95% intervals.
  4. Check interval overlap before treating a dip or rise as a real cohort difference.
  5. Use the data tables for exact cohort counts and small-sample flags.

For example. If recent commit use rises in newer cohorts while any-signal evidence stays flat, newer repositories may be using agents more intensively without a larger share ever showing a trace.

Key terms in this figure

Creation cohort
A group of repositories defined by creation date: the installed base before the study cutoff, or a later creation quarter.
Eligible frame
The repositories this run can legitimately analyse: a usable detection document exists and every selected detection channel succeeded. Repositories outside the frame stay visible in coverage tables but do not enter adoption denominators.
95% Wilson interval
A range around an observed share that accounts for sample size. Small denominators produce wide intervals; a wide interval means the exact value is uncertain.
Detection channel
One way the scanner looks for agent evidence, such as a committed config file, an author or commit trailer, or pull-request metadata. Different channels see different parts of the same usage.

Keep in mind. Newer repositories have had less time to accumulate history, and older ones may be archived or transferred. Cohort patterns describe this frozen snapshot, not a trend over calendar time. Repositories with no recorded creation date (currently CSV-import placeholders) are excluded and counted in the figure subtitle.

Stars vs agent use

Popularity strata are descriptive and not exposure denominators.

Log-binned stratum profile · 95% Wilson intervals for binomial outcomes

Preparing visual…

How to read “Stars vs agent use”

Headline measure

Are popular repositories more likely to show agent use?

What you are looking at

Stars are grouped into log-scaled popularity bands. The chart compares prevalence across those bands under three evidence definitions. Stars measure public attention, not code volume, team size, or adoption intent, so the pattern is descriptive.

How to read it

  1. The horizontal axis runs from few stars to many.
  2. Each line is one evidence definition; isolate a line with the selector when they overlap.
  3. Dots are prevalence and whiskers are 95% intervals.
  4. A rising line means popular repositories are more likely to show agent evidence.
  5. Check whether the pattern holds across all three definitions before trusting it.

For example. If all three lines rise from the lowest to the highest band, the popularity gradient is consistent. If only broad evidence rises, the pattern may reflect more config files rather than more actual use.

Key terms in this figure

Star
GitHub's public bookmark count. Stars measure attention, not code volume, team size, or adoption intent.
95% Wilson interval
A range around an observed share that accounts for sample size. Small denominators produce wide intervals; a wide interval means the exact value is uncertain.
Broad evidence
At least one non-bot detection channel found a trace of the agent. This is the most permissive headline definition.
Strict evidence
Evidence from a behavioural channel (author, commit trailer, or PR metadata) or corroboration from at least two channel families. It is designed to exclude structural traces that may not reflect actual use.

Keep in mind. Popularity correlates with visibility, project type, and contributor count. The gradient is not a causal effect of stars.

Commits vs agent use

Lifetime depth defines the stratum; recent ratios use only inspected eligible commits.

Ordered stratum profile · uncertainty shown for binomial estimates

Preparing visual…

How to read “Commits vs agent use”

Headline measure

Does agent use differ between shallow and deep repositories?

What you are looking at

Repositories are grouped by lifetime default-branch commit count. The first series measure adoption; the last two describe how much of each repository's history the run actually inspected. An adoption number is only credible when the inspected window is large enough to represent the repository.

How to read it

  1. The horizontal axis is an ordered lifetime commit-count band.
  2. The first three lines are different evidence definitions for adoption.
  3. “Median history coverage” is the typical inspected share within a band.
  4. “Full-history coverage” is the share whose inspected window reached the frozen total.
  5. n/a means this run did not record coverage metadata, not that coverage was zero.

For example. A deep-commit band with high adoption but low median coverage may be measuring only a small inspected window. Read it cautiously until coverage is shown to be adequate.

Key terms in this figure

History window
The portion of the default branch that the run actually inspected. History coverage is that window divided by the frozen total commit count.
Coverage
The share of repositories for which a measure could actually be computed. It tells you whether a denominator is trustworthy, not whether adoption is high.
Broad evidence
At least one non-bot detection channel found a trace of the agent. This is the most permissive headline definition.
Strict evidence
Evidence from a behavioural channel (author, commit trailer, or PR metadata) or corroboration from at least two channel families. It is designed to exclude structural traces that may not reflect actual use.

Keep in mind. Commit depth proxies maturity and repository conventions. Large monorepos and small active projects can share a band while differing in how agents are used.

Language vs agent use

Primary-language strata from the frozen source snapshot.

Caterpillar forest plot · point estimate with 95% Wilson interval where defined

Preparing visual…

How to read “Language vs agent use”

Headline measure

How does agent use vary by primary repository language?

What you are looking at

Each row is a primary language from the frozen source snapshot. Prevalence is repo-weighted within language, and the extra series shows which agent has the largest share of observed use there. A single primary label hides repositories that mix several languages.

How to read it

  1. Read down the rows to compare languages; the dot is prevalence.
  2. The line is a 95% interval; wide intervals mean the estimate rests on few repositories.
  3. “Top-agent share” identifies the leading agent within each language.
  4. Use the data tables for exact counts and the full language list.
  5. A high top-agent share means that agent dominates observed traces, not that it is better.

For example. If Python shows 30% prevalence with a top-agent share of 45%, the leading agent accounts for just under half of Python's observed agent evidence.

Key terms in this figure

Eligible frame
The repositories this run can legitimately analyse: a usable detection document exists and every selected detection channel succeeded. Repositories outside the frame stay visible in coverage tables but do not enter adoption denominators.
95% Wilson interval
A range around an observed share that accounts for sample size. Small denominators produce wide intervals; a wide interval means the exact value is uncertain.
Repo-weighted
Every eligible repository counts equally. An owner with 500 repositories contributes 500 times as much as a single-repository owner.
Coding agent
A named AI coding tool or assistant tracked by the corpus. One repository can show evidence for several agents.

Keep in mind. Primary language is one label assigned from the snapshot. Polyglot repositories and generated code can distort the grouping.

Evidence robustness

How much estimated adoption changes under a predeclared stricter evidence rule.

Sensitivity envelope · the broad–strict gap is not a confidence interval

Behavioral 100.0%
Corroborated 100.0%
Structural only 0.0%
Sensitivity gap 0.0 pp

Preparing visual…

How to read “Evidence robustness”

Validity diagnostic

Does the adoption headline survive a stricter definition of evidence?

What you are looking at

The same eligible repositories are scored under several predeclared evidence rules. Broad evidence accepts any non-bot trace; behavioural evidence requires author, trailer, or PR metadata; corroborated evidence requires two channel families; strict evidence combines behavioural and corroborated. The chart shows how much the conclusion depends on the rule.

How to read it

  1. Each row is an evidence definition; the dot is its prevalence.
  2. Whiskers are 95% intervals for the binomial estimate.
  3. The sensitivity gap is broad minus strict, in percentage points.
  4. A small gap means the headline is robust to the rule; a large gap means loose evidence drives it.
  5. Do not interpret the gap as a confidence interval.

For example. If broad is 22% and strict is 14%, eight points of the headline depend on evidence that is structural or uncorroborated. Report that gap alongside the headline.

Key terms in this figure

Broad evidence
At least one non-bot detection channel found a trace of the agent. This is the most permissive headline definition.
Strict evidence
Evidence from a behavioural channel (author, commit trailer, or PR metadata) or corroboration from at least two channel families. It is designed to exclude structural traces that may not reflect actual use.
Detection channel
One way the scanner looks for agent evidence, such as a committed config file, an author or commit trailer, or pull-request metadata. Different channels see different parts of the same usage.
95% Wilson interval
A range around an observed share that accounts for sample size. Small denominators produce wide intervals; a wide interval means the exact value is uncertain.
Sensitivity gap
The difference between two evidence definitions on the same denominator. It is not a confidence interval.

Keep in mind. The rules are fixed before looking at results, but they remain judgement calls. A strict rule can undercount real use that left weak documentation.

Observation and eligibility coverage

The share of every stratum on which each outcome could actually be observed.

Coverage matrix · missing or unselected outcomes are not rendered as zero

Preparing visual…

How to read “Observation and eligibility coverage”

Validity diagnostic

Where can this corpus actually support the adoption estimates?

What you are looking at

Adoption is only meaningful where the data could be observed. This matrix shows, for each stratum, what share of repositories passed each prerequisite: readable, complete channels, successful file scan, valid commit denominator, history observed, and full history. It is a data-quality map, not an outcome measure.

How to read it

  1. Choose a dimension (country, language, star tier, or commit tier) and how many strata to show.
  2. Each column is a coverage measure; each cell is eligible repositories divided by all repositories in that stratum.
  3. Darker cells mean higher coverage.
  4. n/a means the channel was not selected or the run did not record the field.
  5. Low coverage warns that the corresponding outcome is based on a smaller or biased subset, not that adoption is low.

For example. A country with 99% readable coverage but 40% history coverage can support a prevalence estimate, yet its intensity estimates rest on a smaller and possibly biased subset.

Key terms in this figure

Coverage
The share of repositories for which a measure could actually be computed. It tells you whether a denominator is trustworthy, not whether adoption is high.
Eligible frame
The repositories this run can legitimately analyse: a usable detection document exists and every selected detection channel succeeded. Repositories outside the frame stay visible in coverage tables but do not enter adoption denominators.
History window
The portion of the default branch that the run actually inspected. History coverage is that window divided by the frozen total commit count.
Detection channel
One way the scanner looks for agent evidence, such as a committed config file, an author or commit trailer, or pull-request metadata. Different channels see different parts of the same usage.

Keep in mind. High coverage means the denominator is trustworthy; it says nothing about whether adoption is high or low. Coverage can also differ systematically between strata.

Owner-cluster robustness

Repository and owner weighting compared separately for people and organizations.

Paired estimates · intervals resample whole owner clusters when n ≥ 10 owners

Preparing visual…

How to read “Owner-cluster robustness”

Validity diagnostic

Does the answer change when owners rather than repositories are the unit?

What you are looking at

A repository-weighted rate treats every repository equally. An owner-weighted rate first computes each owner's adoption, then treats every owner equally. The chart compares both for GitHub Users and Organizations separately, so a few large owners cannot silently dominate the story.

How to read it

  1. Each account type has two dots: repo-weighted and owner-weighted.
  2. A gap means multi-repository owners pull the repo-weighted result away from the typical owner.
  3. When at least 10 owners exist, whiskers resample whole owner clusters and preserve within-owner dependence.
  4. Read Users and Organizations separately; never pool them into a person-level claim.
  5. Use the data tables for owner counts, repositories per owner, and concentration.

For example. If repo-weighted adoption is 30% but owner-weighted adoption is 12%, a small set of owners with many repositories is driving most of the observed adoption.

Key terms in this figure

Repo-weighted
Every eligible repository counts equally. An owner with 500 repositories contributes 500 times as much as a single-repository owner.
Owner
The GitHub account, either a User or an Organization, that owns a repository. User and Organization results are never pooled.
Eligible frame
The repositories this run can legitimately analyse: a usable detection document exists and every selected detection channel succeeded. Repositories outside the frame stay visible in coverage tables but do not enter adoption denominators.

Keep in mind. Owner clusters model dependence within one account, not dependence across the wider ecosystem. Organizations are not people.

Robust observed debuts

P0, P10, and median observed signal dates reduce dependence on one extreme timestamp.

Percentile timeline · bounded observed dates, not true first-use dates

Preparing visual…

How to read “Robust observed debuts”

Validity diagnostic

When does each agent's observed use begin, without relying on one extreme date?

What you are looking at

For each agent, repositories carrying it contribute one bounded observed date. The chart reports P0, P10, and P50 across those dates, so a single unusually early repository cannot define the debut. Dated coverage shows how many contributing repositories actually had a usable date.

How to read it

  1. P0 is the earliest observed signal, P10 is the 10th percentile, and P50 is the median.
  2. Each dot is one percentile for one agent; read across a row to see the spread.
  3. A large gap between P0 and P50 means the earliest observation is an outlier relative to the typical repository.
  4. Dated coverage is the share of contributing repositories with a usable date.
  5. Compare agents by the median, not by P0 alone.

For example. If P0 is 2023 but P50 is 2025, the agent was first seen in 2023, yet half of its contributing repositories only show it from 2025 onward.

Key terms in this figure

Bounded date
The earliest date observable inside this run's window. It is not an agent's true first use.
Percentile
The value below which a given share of observations fall. P50 is the median; P10 is the value below which 10% fall.
Coverage
The share of repositories for which a measure could actually be computed. It tells you whether a denominator is trustworthy, not whether adoption is high.
Coding agent
A named AI coding tool or assistant tracked by the corpus. One repository can show evidence for several agents.

How to read “Adoption-intensity distribution”

Validity diagnostic

Among repositories that use agents, how heavily do they use them?

What you are looking at

The ECDF plots the whole distribution of commit intensity rather than a few summary bars. Intensity is the share of eligible inspected commits attributed to an agent in each repository. Repositories with zero recent use are excluded from the curve and reported separately, because they answer a different question: whether adoption happened at all.

How to read it

  1. The horizontal axis is intensity from 0% to 100%; the vertical axis is the cumulative share of recent adopters.
  2. A steep rise on the left means most adopters use agents lightly. A curve that stays low and climbs late means a minority use them heavily.
  3. Choose a population from the selector to compare overall, star, commit, cohort, language, or country subsets.
  4. Read the stat strip for P25, P50, P75, P90, zero recent use, and the pervasive share.
  5. Use the curve for shape and the percentiles for exact comparisons.

For example. If the curve reaches 80% by intensity 25%, four out of five recent adopters attribute at most a quarter of their eligible commits to an agent. The heavy tail beyond that is small.

Key terms in this figure

Empirical cumulative distribution
An ECDF plots, for each intensity value, the share of adopters at or below it. It shows the whole distribution without choosing bins.
Commit ratio
The share of eligible inspected commits attributed to an agent. Commits that cannot be attributed, and merge commits where the scanner excludes them, stay outside the denominator.
Pervasive use
At least 20% of eligible inspected commits were attributed to an agent. The threshold is a reporting convention, not a natural boundary.
Eligible frame
The repositories this run can legitimately analyse: a usable detection document exists and every selected detection channel succeeded. Repositories outside the frame stay visible in coverage tables but do not enter adoption denominators.

Keep in mind. The measure conditions on recent adopters with a valid commit denominator. The 20% pervasive threshold is a reporting convention: changing it changes the headline share, not the underlying distribution.

How to read “Multi-agent co-use”

Validity diagnostic

How often do multiple agents appear in the same repository or under the same owner?

What you are looking at

The top strip counts distinct observed agents per detected repository. The tables aggregate each owner's canonical agent union across every repository that owner has in the run. This is about coexistence of traces, not about agents collaborating on one task.

How to read it

  1. Read the strip left to right: 1 agent, 2–5, 6–9, 10+.
  2. A long “1” segment means most detected repositories show a single agent.
  3. Use the account selector to switch between Users and Organizations.
  4. Use the band selector to inspect exact agent sets for owners with a given number of agents.
  5. Rankings are exact sets ordered by owner count; ties break lexically.

For example. If 70% of detected repositories show one agent and the 2–5 band carries most of the rest, multi-agent coexistence is present but not the typical case.

Key terms in this figure

Coding agent
A named AI coding tool or assistant tracked by the corpus. One repository can show evidence for several agents.
Owner
The GitHub account, either a User or an Organization, that owns a repository. User and Organization results are never pooled.
Detected repository
A repository with at least one observed non-bot agent trace, even if it falls outside the fully eligible frame.

Keep in mind. Co-use counts observed traces. It does not prove the agents worked on the same task, at the same time, or with the same intensity, and owner unions span all their repositories in this run.

Whiskers are 95% Wilson intervals unless a panel labels owner-cluster bootstrap intervals; triangle markers flag eligible n < 10. Sensitivity gaps are not confidence intervals. Percentages retain their metric-specific denominator. Missing and unselected observations are never converted to zero. Open Data tables for exact counts and complete rankings.
